title: Act I, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: At the feast of Lupercal a soothsayer warns Caesar to beware the ides of March; Caesar dismisses him. Cassius probes Brutus, who admits he fears the people will choose Caesar for king. Cassius tells how he saved Caesar from drowning and saw him sick with fever, and argues 'the fault... is not in our stars, but in ourselves.' Caesar tells Antony he distrusts Cassius's 'lean and hungry look.' Casca reports that Caesar refused a crown offered three times by Antony and then fell in a fit. Alone, Cassius plans to throw forged letters in Brutus's window.

context.history: The Lupercalia was a February fertility festival. The 'ides' of March was 15 March. Caesar was made dictator for life in early 44 BC, which alarmed defenders of the republic.

significance: This long scene shows Cassius's method of persuasion (flattery, comparison, personal grievance) and Brutus's weak point: his public honor. Caesar's private weaknesses (deafness in one ear, fits) contrast with his public godlike pose.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings” slowly and put it in my own words: Cassius tells Brutus that if they are underlings to Caesar, the fault is in themselves, not in their stars. Next, craft. I notice the contrast between "our stars," meaning fate, and "ourselves," meaning choice, set across a line break for emphasis. The strongest word is “underlings”: it is a contemptuous word for inferiors, chosen to sting Brutus's pride as a Roman noble. Then, effect. How does Cassius use this line to work on Brutus? My answer: Cassius flatters Brutus's sense of honor and freedom to push him toward conspiracy; the line shows his skill as a manipulator and raises the play's question of whether men or fate decide events.
